application.name: Online Examination Platform
application.description: An online examination platform for up to 10000 students. Exams are scheduled in fixed time windows, so many students start and submit at the same moment, then traffic falls back to near zero. Each attempt is timed, answers are saved periodically, submissions must not be lost, and results are published after grading. Data is relational for questions, attempts and results, with uploaded attachments and a question bank.
application.additional_requirements: Answers must be saved every 30 seconds; a submission must never be lost during a network interruption.

architectures.title: Conventional architecture
architectures.summary: A plausible conventional baseline built from the same requirements: resident application servers behind a load balancer, self-managed rails, and a always-on database. It is a comparison point, not a recommendation.

architectures.title: Proposed serverless architecture
architectures.summary: 11 components, 1 function-shaped and 0 placed on a resident runtime. Workload class: spiky request response. The blended score is 78/100 from 10 weighted factors. Favourable: traffic variability (spiky, event-driven demand: capacity follows each event instead of a forecast); request/response shape (median responses of a few hundred milliseconds — a natural function workload); execution duration (all stated operations complete quickly enough for short-lived execution). The workload fits a managed function platform with little architectural compromise. Function-first across the request path, with managed data services.

suitability.headline: Strong candidate for a serverless-first design
suitability.rationale: The blended score is 78/100 from 10 weighted factors. Favourable: traffic variability (spiky, event-driven demand: capacity follows each event instead of a forecast); request/response shape (median responses of a few hundred milliseconds — a natural function workload); execution duration (all stated operations complete quickly enough for short-lived execution). The workload fits a managed function platform with little architectural compromise. Function-first across the request path, with managed data services.

methodology.formula: score = 100 x (0.5 + 0.5 x Σ(weight_i x impact_i)), impact_i in [-1, +1]. Overall = 0.55 x workload score + 0.45 x mean of scored component results (tiers: application and processing; managed services are excluded because their realization is a managed service by definition).

methodology.weight_source: Weights prioritise the factors with the largest documented impact on serverless platform limits: execution duration and traffic variability first, then coupling (state, persistent connections, database connection patterns), then resource/runtime constraints.  They are fixed for this rule pack version so that scores are reproducible and testable, and they are not an industry standard.

security.scope_statement: Architecture-level review of the modelled components and their recorded properties. It is not a penetration test, a vulnerability scan or a certification, and it cannot see configuration that was not described.

baseline_findings.title: Transport security not stated as enforced for a public entry point
baseline_findings.explanation: Nothing in the model requires TLS for a component reachable from the internet, so credentials or tokens could be exchanged in cleartext.
evidence: Web client: transport_security = unspecified
Web server (static assets + reverse proxy): transport_security = unspecified
Load balancer (entry point): transport_security = unspecified
baseline_findings.recommendation: Enforce HTTPS only, redirect plaintext, and enable HTTP strict transport security at the edge.
references: NYX security rule SEC-TLS (docs/METHODOLOGY.md — Security analysis method)

baseline_findings.title: Confidential data without an identified at-rest protection
baseline_findings.explanation: Components holding confidential or restricted data do not record an encryption-at-rest decision, so the strategy cannot be confirmed from the model.
evidence: Identity handled inside the application: data_classification = restricted, encryption_at_rest = None
baseline_findings.recommendation: Enable provider-managed encryption for every store holding this data, and record which key management option (provider-managed or customer-managed) applies.
references: NYX security rule SEC-AT-REST (docs/METHODOLOGY.md — Security analysis method)

baseline_findings.title: Credentials handled outside a dedicated secret store
baseline_findings.explanation: Components that need provider or third-party credentials are modelled as holding them in host configuration, which cannot be rotated, scoped or audited independently.
evidence: Interactive application logic: secrets_handling = environment variables
baseline_findings.recommendation: Move credentials into a managed secret store, use workload identity where available, and rotate on a schedule with an expiry that fails closed.
references: NYX security rule SEC-SECRETS (docs/METHODOLOGY.md — Security analysis method)

methodology: Rules read only recorded component evidence (exposure, authentication, transport security, data classification, encryption, IAM scope, backup policy, secrets handling, audit logging).
A finding requires evidence present in the graph; otherwise the item is reported as a verification gap asking the reviewer to confirm it.
Findings are graded so that severity tracks what the model actually shows: a confirmed public database is high, an unstated TLS policy is medium, an unspecified rotation policy is a question.
3 finding(s) were recorded against the conventional view; those are the issues the proposed design is intended to remove.
limitations: Cannot detect implementation defects, dependency vulnerabilities or misconfigured resources that were not described.
Cannot verify provider-side defaults; each provider's managed defaults are assumed, not proven.
Severity is relative to this model only and is not a CVSS or audit rating.

cost.disclaimer: Relative Infrastructure Cost Units (RICU) are a heuristic index internal to NYX. They are not prices, not currency and not a savings guarantee. 1 RICU = one small always-on compute unit-month.

scenarios.label: Conventional architecture (as-is baseline)
scenarios.description: Capacity is provisioned for the peak and billed continuously; rails are operated by the team.

line_items.label: Application tier — 2 x small instance(s), 24/7
line_items.basis: 2 instance(s) x 1 RICU/instance-month x 1.15 availability factor. Count = ceil(peak 1.5 req/s ÷ 113.6 req/s per instance at 220 ms and 25 concurrent requests each); resident for the whole month whether or not users are present.

line_items.label: Load balancer (entry point)
line_items.basis: 0.12 RICU/month for the provisioned balancer + 0.0067 per 1M requests.

line_items.label: Primary database instance (peak-sized)
line_items.basis: 0.8 RICU/db-month x 1.15; sized for the peak connection and IOPS envelope, so quiet nights still cost the same.

line_items.label: Database storage
line_items.basis: 14 GB x 0.004 RICU per GB-month (same coefficient in both models).

line_items.label: File storage on provisioned volumes
line_items.basis: 40 GB of content plus 25% growth headroom (you must pre-allocate a volume, and filling it blocks the application) x 0.0012 RICU per GB-month.

line_items.label: Cache / session node
line_items.basis: 0.5 RICU/cache-month. Sharing session data across instances needs this extra resident component.

line_items.label: Log capture (files on hosts)
line_items.basis: ~620 bytes per request x 2,574,000 requests at 40% of the managed ingest coefficient, because local files are not centrally indexed (a control gap, not a saving).

line_items.label: Operational maintenance load
line_items.basis: 4 self-managed component(s) x 0.35 RICU of maintenance load (patching, capacity reviews, backup scripts, failover drills). A relative effort proxy, not money.

drivers: Outbound data transfer: 2.8279 RICU (34% of total)
Application tier — 2 x small instance(s), 24/7: 2.3 RICU (28% of total)
Operational maintenance load: 1.4 RICU (17% of total)

scenarios.label: Proposed serverless / hybrid architecture
scenarios.description: Capacity follows executions, with resident capacity kept only where the suitability engine demanded it.

line_items.label: Function execution (request path + async handlers)
line_items.basis: 2,574,000 invocations x 0.0067 RICU per 1M + 283,140 GB-s x 5.6e-07 RICU per GB-s (0.5 GB profile). Nothing is billed while nobody is using the system.

line_items.label: Managed API surface
line_items.basis: 0.12 RICU/month base + 0.033 per 1M requests; authorization and throttling are absorbed here instead of in code.

line_items.label: Managed database (autoscaling capacity)
line_items.basis: Autoscaling floor of 0.56 RICU x 1.15, plus query volume at 0.0067 per 1M. The state is still here — only the capacity model changes.

line_items.label: Database storage
line_items.basis: Identical to the conventional model by construction.

line_items.label: Object storage for artefacts
line_items.basis: 40 GB x 0.0008 RICU per GB-month + request charges. No growth headroom is pre-purchased because capacity is not allocated up front.

line_items.label: Managed cache (shared state, hot reads)
line_items.basis: A smaller node suffices because handlers stay stateless and the API surface fronts hot reads.

line_items.label: Outbound data transfer
line_items.basis: Same volume assumption as the conventional model.

line_items.label: Structured logs, metrics and alarms
line_items.basis: Ingest at 0.0167 RICU per GB + 0.033 for metric and alarm rails. A serverless design leans harder on telemetry, so this line is deliberately not omitted.

line_items.label: Managed identity and secret storage
line_items.basis: Secret store fixed share plus 0.0033 RICU per 1,000 monthly active users x 10,000 users.

line_items.label: Operational maintenance load
line_items.basis: 9 managed component(s) x 0.12 RICU: no OS patching or capacity sizing, but platform limits, IAM and asynchronous failure handling still need design and review.

drivers: Outbound data transfer: 2.8279 RICU (52% of total)
Operational maintenance load: 1.08 RICU (20% of total)
Managed database (autoscaling capacity): 0.6612 RICU (12% of total)

sensitivity.name: Traffic volume
sensitivity.note: The proposed model moves roughly with traffic. The conventional model moves in steps, only when an instance boundary is crossed — a 0.0% delta here means the same instance count still serves the load, which is exactly the elasticity argument.

sensitivity.name: Traffic volume

sensitivity.name: Execution duration
sensitivity.note: Per-request billing makes the proposed model sensitive to duration; resident capacity only changes when slower requests require another instance.

methodology: 1. Quantities come from requirement extraction (users → sessions → requests → peak → jobs); every formula is printed on its line item.
2. Conventional = capacity sized for the peak, billed for the whole month, plus provisioned storage and self-managed rails.
3. Proposed = execution-based charges (invocations, GB-seconds, message counts) plus a smaller fixed floor, plus job-hours for anything the suitability engine kept off the function runtime.
4. Availability multiplies the fixed lines in both models by the same factor.
5. Storage, egress and log volume use identical coefficients in both models on purpose.
6. Model version 2026.10: the numbers are constants in this rule pack, so the version is printed with the result and any change alters the outcome.

components_requiring_modification.change: Move the system of record onto a managed engine with automated backup and pooling
components_requiring_modification.reason: Data movement plus connection-pattern change; the schema is not the hard part, the cutover and connection budget are. It replaces “Primary transactional store (self-managed instance)” in the current design.

components_requiring_modification.change: Port document or key/value access to a managed store and re-key for the real access patterns
components_requiring_modification.reason: A document store rewards access-pattern-first key design; a lift-and-shift of relational queries produces slow reads. It replaces “Document / key-value store (self-managed instance)” in the current design.

components_requiring_modification.change: Externalise session and hot-read state into a managed cache with explicit TTLs
components_requiring_modification.reason: Until state leaves the process, the compute tier cannot be started and stopped per request. It replaces “In-process cache / session memory” in the current design.
compatibility_issues: in-process locks must become atomic cache operations

components_requiring_modification.change: Replace filesystem paths with object keys, signed URLs and lifecycle rules
components_requiring_modification.reason: Any stored path, in-place edit or directory walk becomes an object operation; this touches both code and existing records. It replaces “Uploaded files on the server disk” in the current design.

components_requiring_modification.change: Enable automated snapshots with retention and rehearse a restore
components_requiring_modification.reason: Managed services make the mechanism cheap; the remaining work is agreeing retention and proving the restore. It replaces “Ad-hoc file backup” in the current design.

components_requiring_modification.change: Instrument structured logs, per-use-case metrics and alarms on throttling and dead-letter depth
components_requiring_modification.reason: A managed runtime hides saturation signals; without new alarms, the first incident is discovered by users. It replaces “Log files on each host” in the current design.
compatibility_issues: log volume drives its own cost line

migration.sequencing_rationale: Configuration and storage changes come before code decomposition because they are reversible, independently testable, and they remove the dependencies (local paths, in-process sessions) that make handlers hard to split. Data migration sits before target implementation for the same reason: a new runtime reading the old database shape doubles the risk.

limitations.statement: Generated architectures are conceptual blueprints. NYX does not provision, deploy or modify any cloud account, and a provider switch changes labels only.
Suitability scores come from the versioned local rule pack (2026.10). They are explainable heuristics, not an industry benchmark or a certification.
Cost figures are Relative Infrastructure Cost Units (RICU): a dimensionless index defined inside NYX, not currency, not a provider price list and not a savings guarantee.
The security review is architecture-level only. It is not a penetration test, a vulnerability scan or a compliance audit, and it can only reason about what was described.
Cloud service identities come from a local catalogue snapshot. Limits, quotas, region availability and product names must be re-verified before implementation decisions.
The roadmap deliberately omits durations and person-days: team size, test coverage and code quality are outside this analysis, so any time figure would be invented.
